disease_info: Bipolar II Disorder is characterized by a recurrent course of major depressive episodes and hypomanic episodes, with no history of full manic episodes. Hypomanic episodes involve a distinct period of elevated, expansive, or irritable mood and increased energy lasting at least four days, but without the severe impairment, psychosis, or hospitalization seen in mania. Depressive episodes are often prominent, can be longer and more disabling than the hypomanic periods, and frequently drive help‑seeking. The disorder typically has an episodic course with periods of relative remission, and it can be difficult to distinguish from unipolar depression or cyclothymia without careful assessment of past and subtle hypomanic symptoms.

narrative.personality: Sheena is a meticulous, routine‑oriented and deeply compassionate woman who copes with chronic worry by staying organized and pouring herself into helping others.
narrative.stressor: Over the past year, Sheena’s physical health has become increasingly fragile, with worsening arthritis, reduced mobility, and a recent brief hospitalization after a fall, which disrupted her carefully structured routines and limited her ability to volunteer at the senior center and attend church regularly. As she tried to compensate, she threw herself into organizing programs from home and taking on more phone calls, letters, and grant‑writing than before, staying up late and skipping rest to feel useful and in control. After several weeks of this overextension, she experienced a sharp emotional downturn when she realized she could no longer keep up with her usual level of activity, began cancelling social engagements, and found herself ruminating about being a burden and the future loss of independence. Concerned that her normally resilient, purposeful outlook had given way to a persistent bleakness and that she no longer enjoyed her books, birds, or gardening, her daughter and pastor encouraged her to see a psychiatrist, which she reluctantly agreed to do.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’ve just been feeling so low and empty lately, like there’s no point to anything.”

narrative.personality: Brighton is a hardworking, competitive, and outgoing truck driver who prides himself on discipline and big ambitions, often pushing himself past healthy limits to chase new goals.
narrative.stressor: Brighton’s company recently underwent a reorganization, dangling a possible regional operations manager role that matched his long‑held dream of moving from the cab to the office and eventually building his own refrigerated fleet. In response, he dramatically increased his workload—volunteering for extra routes, hustling for new accounts, and spending his off‑duty hours sketching business plans, researching trucks online, and talking up ideas at tailgates and karaoke nights—leaving almost no time for rest or family. Over several weeks this relentless pace, fueled by his excitement and drive, tipped into a period where he felt constantly keyed‑up and mentally “on,” followed by a crash in which he became increasingly overwhelmed, disorganized with bills and paperwork, and irritable at home and on the road. When his wife noticed that he was lying awake with his mind racing about routes, deals, and what‑ifs nearly every night and that he was snapping at her and their kids, she insisted he see a doctor, and his primary care physician referred him to psychiatry after recognizing a pattern of mood and energy shifts tied to these intense work pushes.
narrative.chief_complaint: “My mind just won’t shut off—my thoughts are going a mile a minute all the time now.”

narrative.personality: Edicta is a curious, creative, and generally laid‑back person who balances careful attention at work with a tendency to procrastinate and drift into artistic daydreams in her personal life.
narrative.stressor: In the past few months, Edicta and her husband have been arguing more intensely about whether and when to have children, finances, and her irregular handling of bills, which has created a tense atmosphere at home despite her usually easygoing nature. In an effort to prove she could be more responsible and to distract herself from the conflict, she began saying yes to extra crossing shifts, taking on a side project designing bilingual safety posters, and staying up late journaling and sketching ideas for murals and community workshops. At first she felt energized by these projects and the sense of purpose, but over several weeks the combination of emotional strain at home and increasing commitments eroded her usual equilibrium, and she started having trouble winding down at night and dragging herself through mornings at her post. After she nearly stepped into the crosswalk later than usual one day because she felt foggy and exhausted, and her husband commented that she seemed “wired and then wiped out” all the time, she agreed to see a mental health professional at her community clinic.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I can’t seem to sleep normally anymore—either I’m up half the night or I wake up feeling like I never really rested.”
